title: Python async (asyncio), Part 6: bounding work: queues and backpressure
tldr: When work arrives faster than it leaves, it piles up at the first line with no limit. During seller-c's outage in a sale, shoppers' refreshes raise arrivals to 3,000 a second against a ranking stage that finishes 2,000: the seller calls stay bounded by Part 3's deadline, but the ranking line grows by 1,000 requests a second, about 410 MB a minute at a measured 7 KB each. This page does that arithmetic with Little's law, then builds the tools: asyncio.Queue bounded and unbounded, put() parked on a Future as backpressure, worker pools with task_done() and join(), Queue.shutdown() (3.13+) and the stop markers used before it, PriorityQueue and LifoQueue. Gateway v7 refuses requests it cannot finish with 'busy' (HTTP's 503 with Retry-After), gives each seller its own cap and a line no longer than what can still finish in time, rate-limits seller-d with a token bucket, and sends audit rows through a bounded queue whose backpressure reaches the front door. Then what breaks: the worker loop that hangs join() forever, a standing queue that answers everything late (60 of 300 on time against 208), limits counted per process at 10 times the load, and clients that retry refusals at once. Ends with Semaphore vs bounded queue vs shedding vs a broker and an interview drill.
